Introduction/AI-SDLC

EDS AI-SDLC

The EDS AI-Software Development Lifecycle connects product ideation, a shared handoff and product implementation. Use this overview to understand how the loops work together, then explore each loop’s practices in detail.

This guide adapts the supplied playbook into a working model for product owners, designers, engineers and reviewers. It describes recommended practices for applying AI to product development within EDS.

Two loops joined by a handoff

The supplied playbook describes two connected learning loops within the AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC). Product ideation is about making the right product: it asks whether the problem is worth solving and whether the proposed solution solves it. Product implementation is about making the product right: it turns validated intent into reliable production behaviour. Each loop has its own work, evidence and decisions.

The handoff centres on a product requirements document (PRD), supported by user interface (UI) artefacts where relevant and current organisational context.

The diagram summarises the relationship between the loops; it does not prescribe a one-way sequence.

The ideation loop repeats until the team can decide on a bounded scope. The PRD records the agreed behaviour; relevant UI artefacts illustrate the experience. Implementation builds and checks that scope. Evidence from delivery and use can reopen an ideation decision, so the handoff does not end collaboration.

The two loops compared
AspectProduct ideationProduct implementation
Question it answersAre we making the right product?Are we making the product right?
Starts fromA problem, user need, strategic priority or new capabilityA validated PRD, UI artefacts and organisational context
LoopThesis, explore, challenge, specify, prototype, measure, learn, decidePlan, slice, implement, verify, release and observe, learn
Main evidenceUser, behavioural and cost evidence from prototypes and testsTests, independent reviews, quality reports and production telemetry
Each pass ends withImprove, redesign, pivot or stop; or hand off when readyAn accepted increment or rework decision; release evidence informs the next refinement
What it improvesThe product intentThe product and the way the team builds it

Explore each loop below, then follow its detailed guidance. Whoever holds decision authority for commitment should be named locally; this guide does not assign it.

The Defence Product Playbook, jointly developed by MINDEF and DSTA, describes a comparable shape for product work. Its ProductOps flywheel runs Research as an outer loop and Design and Test as a fast inner loop. Each turn produces reference artefacts that DevSecOps teams act on concurrently, instead of a locked design handed off once. Read the handoff below in that spirit: it is a working agreement that the loops revisit, not a one-time transfer. The comparison is this guide’s own; the playbook does not describe the AI-SDLC loops.

Sources: [1]; [2]; [5] “Tools to use”.

Product ideation loop

Use ideation when the problem, expected value or proposed experience is uncertain. Bring user observations, operational evidence, alternatives and known constraints.

Move through a product thesis, exploration, challenge, specification, prototyping, measurement, learning and a decision. Repeat the work needed to test the riskiest assumption. A decision can improve the current approach, redesign the solution, pivot to another opportunity or stop the work.

The output is evidence-backed product intent: the problem, expected outcomes, required behaviour and the reasons for choosing them. A commitment decision moves a bounded scope into implementation; a polished prototype alone does not establish readiness.

Explore product ideation: thesis, experiments and decisions.

Source: [1] “From Opportunity to Validated Product Intent” and “Handover to Product Implementation”.

Handoff between the loops

A scope is ready for handoff when the evidence supports the next investment and implementation can work from testable requirements. “Validated” here means supported under the recorded test conditions, not proven for every user or production setting. Discovery continues when new evidence changes the intent.

The PRD records the agreed outcomes, behaviour and constraints. The UI artefacts show how the validated experience should behave and feel. The implementation team decides how to build it within the approved technical and policy constraints.

For a product without a user interface, substitute interface contracts and representative interactions for screens. Keep the evidence and acceptance criteria proportionate to the change.

Assemble the handoff package

  • Product context and outcomes: the target users, problem statement, intended user outcome, business value and strategic fit. Check the problem statement for clarity, consequence, cause and confirmation, the 4C described in product ideation.
  • Prioritised user stories: the user, required behaviour and intended value for the scope to be built.
  • Testable acceptance criteria: positive, negative, edge, permission and failure scenarios that can become tests or evaluations.
  • UI artefacts: approved representative HTML screens and flows covering the core journeys, with a design.md file that records interaction rules, loading, empty, error and permission states, responsive behaviour, accessibility and any intentional deviations.
  • Constraints and dependencies: business rules, non-functional requirements, architecture and data dependencies, and security, privacy, AI and compliance guardrails.
  • Measurement requirements: the value measure and its baseline, success metrics, telemetry, evaluation coverage and guardrail thresholds that implementation needs to instrument.
  • Evidence and decision record: tested assumptions, methods, results, limitations, source links and the authorised commitment decision.
  • Owned ambiguity: open decisions, assumptions, exclusions and deliberate implementation freedoms, each with an owner rather than left silently unclear.

Bring current organisational context into the readiness review: architecture, domain, security, data and operational constraints. Chapter 3 identifies this context alongside the PRD and UI artefacts as the implementation input.

Check readiness

Hand over when:

  1. the highest-risk product assumptions have been tested;
  2. the UI artefacts represent the core user journeys and important states;
  3. acceptance criteria are precise enough to evaluate the implementation;
  4. constraints, guardrails and measurement obligations are explicit; and
  5. remaining ambiguity has a named owner and a plan to resolve it.

Example · fictional handover

After three prototype rounds, the service desk squad’s assistant passes its task-success threshold for password and access requests but not for software requests. The product owner narrows the scope to access requests, records software requests as an exclusion with an owner, and hands over a PRD with acceptance criteria for correct, incomplete and unauthorised requests.

Next step: compare your current PRD with the handover package and readiness checks above, and list the gaps. Read how implementation starts from the PRD and UI artefacts, or read about intent-driven development for ways to record intent and open questions.

These are playbook recommendations; confirm decision authority locally.

Sources: [1] “Handover to Product Implementation”; [2] “Start with an Implementable Definition”.

Product implementation loop

Use implementation when the next change has agreed behaviour and testable acceptance criteria. The team combines the handoff with organisational context, then translates the product requirements document (PRD) into a technical requirements document (TRD) and verifiable tasks.

The six stages are Plan, Slice, Implement, Verify, Release and observe, and Learn. Verification can return a change for rework. Release evidence informs the next refinement; findings can also reopen earlier product or technical decisions.

Each pass improves the product and the way it is built. A defect may need both a code correction and a change to context, tests or review practice to reduce recurrence.

Explore implementation: stage inputs, evidence and exit decisions.

Source: [2] “Run the Six-Stage Product Implementation Loop” and “The loop improves two systems”.

Feed evidence back into the right loop

Compare observed results with the intended user outcome and acceptance criteria. Use the difference to choose the next action, then record what changes and who will follow it through.

  • Behaviour differs from the agreed intent: return to implementation to correct and verify the change.
  • The product works as specified but users do not benefit: revisit ideation to test the problem, experience or value assumptions.
  • The same delivery failure recurs: improve the relevant context, tools, tests or review process and check the next increment.

These routing recommendations apply the feedback principles in Chapters 2 and 3. For a well-understood defect, a bounded issue with acceptance criteria may be enough; the team need not repeat every ideation activity.

DORA recommends making user feedback available to the team and displaying user measures alongside technical measures. Use that evidence to revisit priorities, rather than treating faster output as proof of value.

Diagnose a value measure that stops improving

A stalled measure does not mean the team has failed, but something is holding it back. The Defence Product Playbook suggests finding the cause before changing the plan.

Likely causes of a stalled value measure, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
Likely causeHow you can tellAction
The root cause is not addressedUsers adopt the product, but the problem persistsRevisit the problem statement in ideation
An assumption was falseResearch shows an assumption was wrongPivot the approach in ideation
The problem has changedEvidence shows it shrank or shiftedRedefine or deprioritise the problem
The team is blocked from outsideThe team waits on an approval, decision or access it cannot grant itselfEscalate to whoever holds the blocking decision
The team cannot move fastThe team is active but slow or unfocusedReview its structure, skills and delivery process

A measure that climbs and then flattens may mean the product has delivered the value available to it. Consider moving the product to maintenance and investing in a problem that can still move.

Sources: [3]; [5] “Define the problem, measure the value” and “Govern and review”.

Use AI across the lifecycle

AI-assisted development means using AI to support development work; the resulting product does not need to contain an AI feature. People still decide the intended outcomes, acceptable trade-offs and scope of agent activity.

In ideation, AI can help synthesise research, challenge assumptions and draft prototypes. In implementation, it can help plan tasks, produce changes and collect verification evidence. Review the sources, assumptions and outputs before relying on them.

McKinsey’s February 2025 article describes a broader shift beyond coding assistance: connect discovery and usage evidence, experiment earlier, and address quality, risk and accessibility throughout development. Its expected benefits are industry analysis, not measured outcomes for this guide or EDS.

Hold AI-written work to the same quality bar as any other work. The Defence Product Playbook’s ProductOps Quality Model sets four layers of checks, so that quality does not depend on who or what authored the code:

  1. Prevention, before the build: project rules for agents, reusable design-system components and typed contract boundaries.
  2. Outcome validation, from design onwards: test plans, usability results, scorecards and objectives show whether the work had its intended effect.
  3. Automated scanning, at pull request: composition analysis, static and dynamic scanning and container checks.
  4. Integration verification, after merge: confirmation that the pieces work together.

The playbook’s point is that quality is built in at the first layer, not caught at the scan. Defects found only at the scan gate are found late and at greater cost. Read how implementation applies gates and independent assurance.

Next step: use product ideation to resolve an uncertain opportunity, or product implementation to deliver an agreed change.
